lessonTitle: Binary Isomorphous and Eutectic Phase Diagrams

blocks.text: Lead-tin solder melts at about 183 degrees C when it has about 62 wt% tin, yet pure lead melts at 327 degrees C and pure tin at 232 degrees C. Mixing lowers the melting point, and a phase diagram tells you by how much and what the solid looks like when it freezes.

blocks.markdown: A **binary phase diagram** is a map of the equilibrium phases for every temperature and overall composition of a two-component system at fixed pressure. It tells us which phases are present, their compositions, and how much of each there is. Boundaries on the map are the liquidus (above which everything is liquid), the solidus (below which everything is solid) and the solvus (the solubility limit of one component in a solid phase).

blocks.title: The lever rule
blocks.text: In a two-phase field, draw a horizontal tie line at the temperature of interest. The ends of the tie line give the compositions of the two phases. The mass fraction of each phase is the length of the tie-line segment on the opposite side of the alloy composition divided by the total tie-line length.

blocks.caption: $C_0$: overall alloy composition; $C_\alpha$, $C_\beta$: phase compositions at the tie-line ends (all in wt% of one component). $W_\alpha+W_\beta=1$.

blocks.title: Lever rule in an isomorphous Cu-Ni alloy
blocks.prompt: A Cu-35 wt% Ni alloy at 1250 degrees C lies in the liquid + $\alpha$ field. The tie line read from the Cu-Ni diagram gives $C_L=31.5$ wt% Ni and $C_\alpha=42.5$ wt% Ni (approximate diagram readings). Find the mass fractions of liquid and $\alpha$.

steps.text: Fraction liquid is the segment on the $\alpha$ side of the alloy composition over the tie line.

blocks.answer: 68 percent liquid (31.5 wt% Ni) and 32 percent $\alpha$ (42.5 wt% Ni).

blocks.markdown: **Eutectic systems.** When two components have limited solid solubility in each other, the liquidus curves slope down from the two melting points and meet at the *eutectic point*, the lowest temperature at which liquid exists. The alloy of eutectic composition freezes at that single temperature into a fine mixture of two solid phases. In a *simplified eutectic system* used here, component A forms an $\alpha$ solid solution (at most 10 wt% B at the eutectic temperature) and component B forms a $\beta$ solid solution (at most 90 wt% B), with the eutectic at 40 wt% B. These numbers are illustrative, not those of a specific alloy.

rows: Some bronzes and steels at high temperature
blocks.caption: Three invariant reactions on binary diagrams: each occurs at a fixed temperature and composition.
Gibbs phase rule at constant pressure: $F$ degrees of freedom, $C$ components, $P$ phases.

blocks.markdown: At the eutectic temperature $C=2$ and $P=3$ ($L$, $\alpha$, $\beta$), so $F=0$: the reaction is invariant, which is why a pure eutectic alloy freezes at a single temperature with a thermal arrest on its cooling curve.

blocks.title: Microstructure of a hypoeutectic alloy
blocks.prompt: In the simplified eutectic system, a 25 wt% B alloy is cooled slowly from the liquid. Describe the path, and find the fractions of primary $\alpha$ and eutectic constituent and the total fractions of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ just below the eutectic temperature.

steps.text: Path: liquid, then liquid + primary $\alpha$, then at the eutectic temperature the remaining liquid (40 wt% B) transforms to $\alpha+\beta$.
Just above the eutectic temperature the tie line runs from $\alpha$ (10) to $L$ (40): primary $\alpha=(40-25)/(40-10)=0.50$ and eutectic constituent $=0.50$.
Just below the eutectic temperature the tie line runs from $\alpha$ (10) to $\beta$ (90): total $\alpha=(90-25)/(90-10)=0.8125$.
Total $\beta=(25-10)/(90-10)=0.1875$, all of it in the eutectic.

blocks.answer: 50 percent primary $\alpha$ and 50 percent eutectic; in terms of phases 81.25 percent $\alpha$ and 18.75 percent $\beta$.

items: Choose the tie line at the temperature of interest; the lever rule is valid only in a two-phase field.
Use the tie line just above the eutectic temperature for primary and eutectic constituents, and just below for total phases.
Hypoeutectic alloys (below the eutectic composition) have primary $\alpha$; hypereutectic alloys have primary $\beta$.
Peritectic and eutectoid reactions are invariant, too; each has three phases at a single temperature.

blocks.title: Phases and constituents differ
blocks.text: A phase has a fixed composition and structure ($\alpha$ or $\beta$). A constituent is what you see in the microstructure, such as primary $\alpha$ or the eutectic mixture. Fractions of phases and of constituents come from different tie lines.

points: The lever rule gives the mass fractions of the two phases from a tie line in a two-phase field.
A eutectic reaction is $L\rightarrow\alpha+\beta$, a peritectic is $L+\alpha\rightarrow\beta$, and a solvus is a solid-solubility limit line.
Cooling a hypoeutectic alloy forms primary $\alpha$ first, then the remaining liquid turns to eutectic at a fixed temperature.

questions.stem: Which statement defines a eutectic reaction in a binary system?

options.text: On cooling, one liquid phase transforms isothermally into two different solid phases
On cooling, one solid phase transforms into two other solid phases
On cooling, a liquid and a solid react to form a different single solid
On cooling, a single liquid solidifies to a single solid of the same composition

questions.correctOptionText: On cooling, one liquid phase transforms isothermally into two different solid phases

distractorRationale.a: Correct: $L\rightarrow\alpha+\beta$ at a fixed temperature and composition.
distractorRationale.b: This is a eutectoid reaction, in which both parent and products are solid.
distractorRationale.d: This is congruent freezing of a pure component or congruent melting compound, not a eutectic.

questions.explanation: A eutectic is an invariant reaction in which a liquid of eutectic composition transforms on cooling to two solid phases simultaneously, $L\rightarrow\alpha+\beta$. It occurs at a single temperature, the lowest temperature at which liquid exists in the system.

questions.stem: On a binary phase diagram, a peritectic reaction on cooling is written as:

options.text: $L+\alpha\rightarrow\beta$
$L\rightarrow\alpha+\beta$
$\gamma\rightarrow\alpha+\beta$
$\alpha+\beta\rightarrow L$

distractorRationale.a: Correct: a liquid and a solid phase react to give a new solid phase at a fixed temperature.
distractorRationale.d: This is melting on heating, the reverse of a eutectic reaction.

questions.explanation: In a peritectic reaction, a liquid and a solid phase react on cooling to form a different solid phase at a single temperature. It is easily confused with the eutectic, where one liquid splits into two solids.

questions.stem: A hypothetical isomorphous A-B system has, at a given temperature, a tie line whose ends are at $C_L=20$ wt% B (liquid) and $C_\alpha=45$ wt% B (solid). An alloy of overall composition 38 wt% B is held at that temperature. Using the lever rule, calculate the percentage of the alloy that is solid $\alpha$.
questions.explanation: The fraction of $\alpha$ is the segment from the alloy composition to the liquid end, divided by the whole tie line: $W_\alpha=(C_0-C_L)/(C_\alpha-C_L)=(38-20)/(45-20)=0.72$. So 72 percent of the alloy is $\alpha$ and 28 percent is liquid.

questions.stem: Take a simplified eutectic system with a $\alpha$ phase (maximum 10 wt% B) and a $\beta$ phase (maximum 90 wt% B) both in equilibrium at the eutectic temperature. An alloy with 70 wt% B is cooled slowly to just below the eutectic temperature. Calculate the percentage of $\beta$ in the microstructure, counting all of it, including that in the eutectic.
questions.explanation: Just below the eutectic temperature the tie line runs from $\alpha$ (10 wt% B) to $\beta$ (90 wt% B). The fraction of $\beta$ is $(C_0-10)/(90-10)=(70-10)/80=0.75$, so 75 percent of the alloy is $\beta$ and 25 percent is $\alpha$.

questions.stem: In the simplified eutectic system with eutectic composition 40 wt% B, $\alpha$ phase up to 10 wt% B and $\beta$ phase up to 90 wt% B at the eutectic temperature, an alloy of 60 wt% B is cooled slowly to just below the eutectic temperature. Calculate the percentage of the structure that is the eutectic mixture (the part that was liquid immediately above the eutectic temperature).
questions.explanation: Immediately above the eutectic temperature, the alloy at 60 wt% B is liquid (40 wt% B) plus primary $\beta$ (90 wt% B). The primary $\beta$ fraction is $(60-40)/(90-40)=0.40$, so the liquid that transforms to eutectic is $0.60$, or 60 percent.

questions.stem: A binary eutectic alloy of 25 wt% B (hypoeutectic) is cooled slowly from the liquid. Which sequence of microstructural events is correct?

options.text: Liquid, then liquid + primary $\alpha$, then primary $\alpha$ + eutectic mixture of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ at the eutectic temperature
Liquid, then entirely $\alpha+\beta$ eutectic at the liquidus temperature
Liquid, then entirely $\alpha$ at the eutectic temperature
Liquid, then primary $\beta$, then eutectic

questions.correctOptionText: Liquid, then liquid + primary $\alpha$, then primary $\alpha$ + eutectic mixture of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ at the eutectic temperature

distractorRationale.a: Correct: primary $\alpha$ forms first, then the remaining liquid reaches the eutectic composition and transforms.
distractorRationale.b: Only the alloy at the eutectic composition becomes fully eutectic; at other compositions primary solid forms first.
distractorRationale.c: The alloy is outside the single-phase $\alpha$ field at the eutectic temperature, so $\beta$ eventually forms.
distractorRationale.d: Primary $\beta$ forms in hypereutectic alloys, with compositions above the eutectic.

questions.explanation: A hypoeutectic alloy first crosses the liquidus into a liquid plus $\alpha$ region, where primary $\alpha$ grows and the liquid becomes enriched in B. At the eutectic temperature the remaining liquid has the eutectic composition and transforms to $\alpha+\beta$.

questions.stem: What is a solvus line on a binary phase diagram?

options.text: The boundary showing the solubility limit of one component in a solid phase as a function of temperature
The boundary above which the alloy is entirely liquid
The boundary below which the alloy is entirely solid
The horizontal line at the eutectic temperature

questions.correctOptionText: The boundary showing the solubility limit of one component in a solid phase as a function of temperature

distractorRationale.a: Correct: it separates a single solid-solution field from a two-phase solid field.
distractorRationale.d: This is the eutectic isotherm, an invariant line.

questions.explanation: The solvus marks the limit of solid solubility, typically falling with decreasing temperature, so that a solid solution cooled across it becomes supersaturated and precipitates a second phase. This is the basis of precipitation hardening.

questions.stem: For a binary system at constant pressure, the Gibbs phase rule is $F=C-P+1$. How many degrees of freedom does the system have during the eutectic reaction $L\rightarrow\alpha+\beta$?

options.text: 0, because three phases coexist and $C=2$
1, because two components exist
2, because temperature and composition can both vary
3, because three phases coexist

distractorRationale.a: Correct: $F=2-3+1=0$, so temperature and compositions are all fixed.
distractorRationale.b: One degree of freedom would apply if only two phases coexisted, as in a two-phase field.
distractorRationale.c: Temperature and phase compositions are fixed in an invariant reaction.
distractorRationale.d: The number of phases subtracts from the degrees of freedom, not adds to them.

questions.explanation: With two components ($C=2$) and three coexisting phases ($P=3$), the rule gives $F=2-3+1=0$ degrees of freedom. The reaction is invariant: it proceeds at a single temperature with fixed phase compositions, which shows as a thermal arrest on a cooling curve.

questions.stem: Describe, with the aid of a labelled sketch in words, the cooling path and final microstructure of an alloy of exactly the eutectic composition cooled slowly from the liquid, and contrast it with a hypoeutectic alloy. Say what the lever rule shows for the phase fractions just below the eutectic temperature.
markingGuide: Eutectic alloy remains liquid until the eutectic temperature, with no primary phase (1 mark)
At the eutectic temperature the liquid transforms isothermally into two solids $\alpha+\beta$ (1 mark)
The microstructure is a fine, often lamellar, mixture of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ (1 mark)
Hypoeutectic alloy first forms primary $\alpha$ over a range of temperature, in the liquid + $\alpha$ field (2 marks)
Remaining liquid reaches the eutectic composition and transforms to eutectic (1 mark); final structure is primary $\alpha$ in a eutectic matrix (1 mark)
Lever rule on the tie line below the eutectic temperature gives the total fractions of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ (1 mark)
questions.explanation: A eutectic alloy solidifies completely at one temperature into a fine mixture of the two solids. A hypoeutectic alloy first rejects primary $\alpha$, then the leftover liquid becomes eutectic, giving primary $\alpha$ in a eutectic matrix.

questions.stem: In the simplified eutectic system (eutectic composition 40 wt% B; $\alpha$ up to 10 wt% B and $\beta$ up to 90 wt% B at the eutectic temperature) an alloy of 20 wt% B is cooled slowly to just below the eutectic temperature. Calculate (a) the mass fraction of primary $\alpha$, (b) the mass fraction of eutectic constituent, and (c) the total mass fractions of $\alpha$ and $\beta$.
markingGuide: Primary $\alpha$ (formed above the eutectic temperature) $=(40-20)/(40-10)=0.667$ (2 marks)
Checks that all the $\beta$ lies in the eutectic: $0.333\times(40-10)/(90-10)=0.125$ (1 mark)
questions.explanation: The two tie lines are used at different temperatures: just above the eutectic temperature (alpha plus liquid) for the primary and eutectic constituents, and just below it (alpha plus beta) for total phase fractions. Both give consistent results, since the $\beta$ is only in the eutectic.
